title: SRE Standards: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
content:
Overview

This document codifies Redwood Inference's SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review expectations, operational tooling, and canonical SRE runbooks. The goal is to provide a single reference for on-call engineers, service owners, and platform teams so that reliability work is consistent, measurable, and actionable.

Scope and intent
- Applies to all externally-facing production services (hosted API, control plane, dedicated pools) and critical internal platform services (orchestration, billing, telemetry).
- Emphasizes measurable SLOs, clear error budget policies, repeatable capacity planning, and high-quality post-incident reviews.
- Balances customer-facing availability targets with business cost/throughput goals.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

Principles
- SLOs measure user-facing correctness or latency; they are the primary signal for reliability decisions.
- Every production service must define an owner, at least one SLO, a measurement method, and a review cadence.
- Error budgets are the operational allowance for risk. When burn exceeds thresholds, mitigations (rate limits, throttles, rollbacks) must be considered.

Required metadata for each SLO
1. Service name (e.g., inference-api)
2. Owner (team and single primary)
3. SLO definition (metric, window, target)
4. Measurement source (prometheus rule / synthetic check / tracing)
5. Alerting thresholds (warning/critical)
6. Error budget policy and escalation steps
7. Review cadence (monthly for stable services; weekly for high-burn)

Example SLOs
- inference-api availability: 99.9% success rate for production text-generation requests measured over a 30-day rolling window (success = HTTP 2xx and response latency <= 1.2s for 95th percentile).
- model-serving-latency: 95th percentile latency <= 300ms for embeddings requests measured over a 7-day window (for dedicated pool customers).

Error budget policy (example)
| Error budget remaining | Action | Owner | Timeline |
|-----------------------|--------|-------|----------|
| >= 50% | Normal operations; follow standard deploy checklist | Service owner | Continuous
| 20% - 50% | Notify owner and product; prepare mitigation plan; pause non-critical riskier changes | Service owner + Product | 48 hours
| 5% - 20% | Halt feature rollouts; require merged mitigation plan and SRE sign-off for changes | Service owner + SRE | 24 hours
| < 5% | Initiate emergency throttle/rollback strategy; escalate to on-call lead and engineering execs | SRE on-call + Eng manager | Immediate (page)

Error budget burn detection and alerts
- Metrics: use Prometheus recording rules for SLO windows. SLI -> SLO -> ErrorBudget calculation exported to a dedicated errorbudget dashboard.
- Alerts: two alerts are required per SLO: Warning (e.g., remaining <= 50%) and Critical (remaining <= 20%). Critical fires a high-priority PagerDuty page.

2) Capacity planning and autoscaling guidance

Principles
- Capacity planning must tie to real customer workloads, not theoretical peaks. Use p95/p99 traffic forecasts and token-per-request distribution.
- Maintain a buffer (safety margin) sized by SLA and business tolerance: default safety margin = 40% for inference pools with mixed customers; lower (20%) for dedicated pools with committed capacity.

Quarterly capacity planning process (high level)
1. Collect 90/95/99 traffic percentiles, token distribution, and model mix from the last 90 days.
2. Forecast growth (conservative/likely/aggressive) and map to expected GPU/CPU / pod counts by workload.
3. Identify resource-constrained services and expected contention points (KV cache size, memory, PCIe for multi-GPU).
4. Define mitigations (autoscale policies, burst pools, spillover routing to cheaper models).
5. Create a runway plan: procure / provision nodes, schedule maintenance windows, and communicate to stakeholders.

Autoscaling guardrails
- Horizontal autoscaling: scale by replica count for stateless controllers where possible; target p95 queue latency < defined threshold.
- Vertical or instance-level scaling: used for model-serving pods where GPU attachment is required; prefer instance pools to avoid node churn.
- Burst capacity: configure separate burst pools (lower priority, preemptible) with automatic fallback routing.

Capacity thresholds to instrument (examples)
- GPU utilization (p95 per shard) > 80% triggers warning.
- KV cache hit rate drop of > 10% correlating with latency increase triggers investigation.
- Average queue wait time > 200ms for > 5 minutes triggers paging.

3) Reliability initiatives and investment prioritization

README for reliability OKRs
- Each quarter, product and SRE must align on top reliability initiatives (e.g., prefix cache improvements, better fallback model routing, catalog of quantization-safe models).
- Prioritization criteria: customer-visible impact, error-budget savings, operational cost reduction, and implementation effort.

Examples of high-value initiatives
- Prefix/KV cache sharding to reduce tail latency for long-context generation.
- Model fallback graph: automated downgrade path when primary model capacity is constrained.
- Streaming response stability: reduce connection resets by 90% for streaming endpoints.

4) Incident review standards and post-incident process

Goals
- Fast, blameless learning and clear, actionable remediation.
- Consistent RCA quality so that similar incidents are prevented.

Timeline and required deliverables
1. Detection and triage: on-call pages and incident commander assigned within 10 minutes of critical alert.
2. Initial postmortem draft: incident commander publishes a short incident summary within 48 hours.
3. Full RCA: completed within 7 business days and includes timeline, impact, root cause, contributing factors, corrective actions, and owners.
4. Follow-up review: SRE lead verifies mitigation completion; re-open the postmortem if mitigations are incomplete after 30 days.

RCA quality checklist
- Timeline with clocked events (UTC).
- Quantified impact (requests, error budget burned, customer-facing metrics).
- Root cause statement in one sentence.
- Contributing factors (3-5 bullets).
- Corrective actions (short-term and long-term) with owners and due dates.
- Preventive checks (synthetic tests, alerts) added as part of the mitigation.

Severity taxonomy and reporting
- Sev1: Customer-impacting outage affecting >10% of traffic or major customers; immediate exec notification; full RCA required.
- Sev2: Degraded service affecting a significant subset; RCA required within 7 days.
- Sev3: Minor-impact incident; operational note and learnings recorded.

5) Operational tooling and dashboards

Core tooling list (approved)
- Metrics: Prometheus (recording rules for SLIs/SLOs), Thanos for long-term metrics retention.
- Dashboards: Grafana (SLO overview, per-service perf, capacity).
- Logs: Loki (indexed by trace_id / request_id), structured JSON logs for inference requests.
- Tracing: Jaeger / Tempo with sampling for production inference requests.
- Alerting & paging: Alertmanager + PagerDuty for on-call.
- Incident management: Confluence for postmortems; linear/jira for tracking mitigations.

Standard dashboards to maintain
- SLO Overview: single pane showing all services with current error budget remaining and burn rate.
- Capacity heatmap: GPU utilization, pod counts, pod queue latency by shard.
- Model performance: p50/p95/p99 latency per model family and per region.
- Paging health: list of active alerts, mean time to acknowledge (MTTA), mean time to resolve (MTTR).

Operational runbooks (stable home)
- Keep runbooks checked into Confluence and linked in the on-call PagerDuty rota.
- Each runbook must indicate last test date. Runbook content must be validated at least quarterly.

6) Canonical SRE runbook template and examples

Runbook template (required fields)
- Runbook title
- Service affected
- Owner and escalation path (names + PagerDuty escalation)
- Symptoms and detection (alerts / dashboards)
- Immediate mitigation steps (1-5) with expected effect
- Diagnostics commands and queries (promql, kubectl, grpc curl)
- Recovery steps and rollback plan
- Post-incident actions and links to RCA template

Example runbook: Inference API high tail latency
- Title: inference-api-high-tail-latency
- Service: inference-api (prod)
- Owner: inference-platform team (primary: oncall-inference)
- Symptoms: p95 latency > 1.2s OR increased 5xx rate > 0.5% for 5 minutes
- Detection: Grafana alert: inference_api_latency_p95 > 1.2s for 5m (critical)

Immediate mitigation steps
1. Check SLO dashboard and error budget remaining for inference-api.
2. Run PromQL to find hot models and regions (example):
   promql: sum by (model, region) (rate(inference_request_count{job="inference-api",status!~"2.."}[5m]))
3. If a single model or shard is overloaded: divert traffic to fallback model (routing knob) or scale the serving pool:
   - kubectl scale deployment inference-model-foo --replicas=+2 -n inference-prod
4. If global congestion: enable emergency throttling at API gateway:
   - curl -X POST https://config.redwood.internal/api/throttle -d '{"service":"inference-api","qps":1000}'
5. If deployment recently rolled: roll back to previous revision via deployment history.

Diagnostics commands (examples)
- kubectl get pods -n inference-prod -l app=inference --sort-by=.status.startTime
- kubectl logs <pod> -c inference-runtime --since=1h | jq '.latency_ms' | sort -nr | head
- promql for queue latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(inference_queue_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le))

Recovery and verification
- Verify p95 latency returns below SLO for 15 minutes and error rate normalizes.
- Confirm that error budget burn slows (dashboard).
- If recovery requires capacity changes, open a capacity run and notify product and SRE leads.

Post-incident actions
- Open incident postmortem in Confluence using the RCA template link.
- Assign corrective action owners with due dates; add SLO checks and synthetic tests as appropriate.
- Schedule a follow-up review 30 days after incident to validate long-term mitigation.

7) Governance, review cadence, and training

Governance
- SLOs must be reviewed at least quarterly by service owners and SRE leads. Major SLO changes require an RFC and SRE approval.
- Error budget burn above 50% for two consecutive weeks triggers an operational review with product and finance (cost implications).

Training and exercises
- Run quarterly game days focused on high-impact failure modes (e.g., cache loss, model fallback failure, regional outage).
- On-call training: all new engineers scheduled for shadow on-call rotations with a checklist before primary on-call ownership.
